name: Trigger point therapy for neck and jaw

lead: Trigger point therapy applies sustained pressure, stretching or massage to small tender spots inside tight bands of muscle, such as the upper trapezius in the neck and the masseter in the jaw. In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed as a way to release jaw clenching and neck tension, with the hoped-for payoff of a more relaxed jaw, better head and shoulder posture and less facial tightness.

The technique comes from the work of physician Janet Travell and David Simons, and is practised today by physiotherapists, massage therapists and, in Australia, regulated myotherapists. Manual trigger point therapy is one of the interventions that a 2023 BMJ guideline panel recommended for chronic temporomandibular disorder pain, while the broader trigger point concept remains debated among researchers.

paras: Practitioners locate a tender nodule in a muscle and apply sustained pressure, then often add stretching or exercises. People also use thumbs, a ball or a handheld tool on their own neck, shoulders and jaw muscles. Routines usually run a few minutes per spot and are repeated over weeks, often alongside posture work or jaw relaxation habits.

Manual pressure is generally low-risk, though it can leave soreness or bruising. Wikipedia notes that treatment over the masseter may affect the salivary glands lying just beneath it, and that injection-based variants such as dry needling carry additional risks. Persistent jaw, neck or head pain can have causes other than muscle knots and is usually assessed by a clinician.

web.title: Trigger point therapy for neck and jaw — Grokipedia

chain: Pressure and stretching on tight neck and jaw muscles
Easier head, neck and jaw posture and a more relaxed facial expression
angle.text: People use trigger point work to loosen the muscles that hold the jaw clenched and the neck forward. The appearance payoff they describe is a more relaxed face and better head posture rather than a structural change.

lead: Trigger point therapy for the neck and jaw is the practice of pressing on, stretching or massaging small tender spots in tight muscle bands, called myofascial trigger points, in muscles such as the upper trapezius, the neck extensors and the masseter and temporalis of the jaw. Practitioners and self-treaters aim to reduce tension and pain, restore range of motion and soften habitual clenching. [1][2]

People interested in their appearance use it for a chain of effects: a looser jaw and neck can make a clenched, strained facial expression less pronounced, can make it easier to hold the head and shoulders in a better posture, and can help someone keep up jaw and neck training or posture routines. These are goals that practitioners and community members describe; the research on the therapy itself concerns pain and function. [1][3]

The concept originates with American physician Janet Travell, who published the term myofascial trigger point in 1942 and later co-authored a major reference with David Simons. [2][4] A non-injection form of the approach was developed by Bonnie Prudden in the 1970s under the name myotherapy, which is a regulated allied health profession in Australia. [2] A 2023 BMJ practice guideline recommended manual trigger point therapy among interventions for chronic temporomandibular disorder pain. [5] Whether trigger points exist as a distinct physical finding is debated, and a 2015 review in Rheumatology called the concept baseless, which proponents disputed. [4]
infobox: Myofascial trigger points in neck, shoulder and jaw muscles

paras: A myofascial trigger point is described as a hyperirritable spot in a taut band of skeletal muscle. Pressing on it can produce local tenderness, a twitch response or pain felt elsewhere, called referred pain. [4] In the neck and jaw, commonly discussed sites include the upper trapezius, the muscles at the back of the neck, and the masseter and temporalis used for chewing. [4][4]

Treatment methods include ischemic compression, where sustained pressure is held on the spot, along with massage, stretching and exercise. Injection-based approaches such as dry needling or local anaesthetic are separate, clinician-delivered variants. [4]

Descriptions of painful muscle knots go back to the 19th century, and Janet Travell popularised the modern concept from the 1940s. [4] Grokipedia describes Bonnie Prudden's 1970s myotherapy as a non-injection adaptation of Travell and Simons' work that emphasised compression applied by the practitioner or the patient. [2]

Today myotherapy is a named profession in Australia, and trigger point work is also offered by physiotherapists, chiropractors and massage therapists. [2][4] Online appearance communities discuss it mainly in connection with jaw clenching and neck posture.

Community members who focus on the jaw describe tight masseters and a forward neck posture as contributors to a tense look, and describe pressure on the muscles as part of routines alongside posture work and jaw relaxation. The sources describe these as individual practices and anecdotes rather than a defined protocol.

A 2023 BMJ clinical practice guideline on chronic pain associated with temporomandibular disorders issued strong recommendations, compared with placebo or sham, for several non-drug options, including manual trigger point therapy and supervised jaw exercise and stretching with or without manual trigger point therapy. [5] The accompanying systematic review and network meta-analysis covered 153 trials with 8,713 participants and 59 interventions. [6]

A 2022 systematic review and meta-analysis of manual and exercise therapy for cervicogenic headache included trigger point therapy among the manual approaches studied across 20 trials with 1,439 patients. [7] Older reviews describe trigger point therapy together with exercise as part of managing myofascial pain and masticatory myofascial pain. [3][1]

Wikipedia summarises that manual therapy shows moderate evidence for short-term relief, that examination for trigger points has been reported as unreliable, and that the existence of the trigger point itself remains contested. [4] These studies concern pain and function; no trial has tested trigger point therapy for facial appearance.

Pressure can leave temporary soreness. Wikipedia notes that treatment over the masseter may injure the salivary glands just beneath it and that invasive variants can damage soft tissue. [4] Persistent jaw or neck pain, clicking or limited opening is the kind of symptom clinicians evaluate for temporomandibular or other causes. [5]
